extracted.intended_audience: students and authors writing mathematical exposition, textbooks, and literate programs (mathematicians and computer scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing, typesetting, and presenting mathematics, algorithms, and literate programs — covering prose style, formula layout, notation, modules, and book preparation. Aimed at authors preparing papers, textbooks, exercises, and program documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector notation choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an appropriate notation for vectors in context (e.g., boldface symbols or arrows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either boldface symbols or arrows over vectors are appropriate depending on the context; be consistent and pick the form suitable to your audience and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use roman type for ordinal suffixes
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a raised 'st' in phrases such as 'the 1st component', use roman type (upright) rather than italic/math type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid typesetting the 'st' as a mathematical superscript; render ordinal suffixes in roman text to make it clear you're not speaking of an exponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid psychologically bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't place the final symbol of a sentence or expression on a different line from the rest of its sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonbreaking spaces (e.g., a tilde ~ in TeX) or processor-specific methods to prevent undesirable breaks that confuse reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who are not strong spellers should learn to use spelling checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many people are better at spelling than others; use tools to avoid simple orthographic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep formulas manageable (name and conquer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting formulas get so long that they don't format well or become unnecessarily confusing; break or rename subexpressions so units remain readable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new symbols or restructure expressions so components remain as coherent units. Long formulas that are repeatedly manipulated should be given names or split to preserve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks sparingly; excessive quoting ('Three cute things in quotes') can be distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve quotes for necessary cases; avoid overusing them for emphasis or stylistic coyness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive or awkward subscripts which reduce readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose notation so that subscripts do not become unreadable or ambiguous (example: prefer Pi ∈ P rather than awkward stacked subscripts); consider renaming to reduce nesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of results in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words like 'Theorem' and 'Lemma' when they appear in numbered titles (e.g., Lemma 1, Theorem 23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventional capitalization for named/numbered results to aid clarity and indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert words between adjacent formulas to avoid ambiguity (avoid constructions like 'Add k times to c.' where intent is unclear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure English words separate or clarify formula fragments so the reader does not misparse commands or statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before or very near use
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them, or at least very close to their first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long spans of text where a symbol appears without definition; local placement of definitions helps comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence openings; avoid monotonous starters
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get stuck using a small set of sentence starters repeatedly (e.g., Thus, Consequently, Therefore, And so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variety in sentence structure to avoid monotony, but preserve parallelism when that is the rhetorical point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences comprehensible left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences so the reader can understand them as they read left-to-right; avoid constructions that temporarily misassign grammatical roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, write 'We prove that the two conditions (grunt) and (snort) imply (blah)' rather than 'We prove that (grunt) and (snort) implies (blah),' which misleads the reader initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'that' by cadence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines exist for the use of the word 'that', but final placement must be dictated by cadence and clarity; read aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose inclusion or omission of 'that' based on how the sentence sounds and its clarity when spoken aloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-sensitive diction (e.g., 'shall')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words (like 'shall') may be natural in definitions for some readers but formal for younger audiences; choose vocabulary mindful of audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust formality depending on target readers; be consistent and intentional in tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in mathematical wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise terms: e.g., if you mean 'not nonincreasing' do not say 'increasing' as they mean different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small logical differences matter; ensure mathematical adjectives and quantifiers express exactly what you intend (examples given with Pi and Pj indices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active phrasing ('A proof shows...') to passive ('It can be shown...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active voice often increases clarity and directness; replace passive constructions when they obscure the agent or make prose vaguer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep tense consistent for the same subject within a sentence or closely related sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions like 'We assume now..., hoping to show...' over disjointed tense mixes like 'We assume now..., and will show that...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrase proofs by contradiction clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clumsy phrases like 'Assume by contradiction that (blah)'; instead say 'The proof that (blah) is by contradiction' or 'To prove (grunt), let us assume the opposite and see what happens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, reader-friendly wording to introduce proof techniques rather than stilted formulaic phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational tone with signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone with signposts and clear transition paragraphs improves readability of proofs and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small informal remarks ('The operative word is zero', 'The lemma is half proved') and explicit division of proof parts aid reader navigation and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent and reader-friendly in relational notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose relational notation that is easy for the reader to visualize and keep index ordering consistent (e.g., Pi < Pj vs. explicit pair representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the form that matches the prior exposition and is easiest for visualization; keep the relative positions of indices consistent across text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professionals for book production
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the value of book designers and copy editors in typesetting, fonts, margins, and overall page design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author self-publishing should still consider professional services for polish; designers influence page plans, equation placement, and typography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite in multiple passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft, then edit repeatedly — writing by hand first can match thought speed and successive passes reveal different issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's sequence: pencil draft, type while editing for flow, TeX stage with further passes; different passes reveal different problems (flow, layout, typesetting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate mathematical numerals from text numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: When using fonts like Euler, distinguish mathematical numerals (e.g., zero with apex point) from text/date numerals in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful during book preparation to indicate where numerals are mathematical versus part of the prose so typesetters use the correct glyphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words by ear and refine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some choices ('all' vs 'all of', position of 'only'/'also') are determined by what sounds best; edit for rhythm and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment during editing and keep shifting words until flow and meaning are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break long formulas logically and consider symbol introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When long formulas don't fit, break lines logically or introduce new symbols to make display less jarring; sometimes move from inline to displayed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line-break rules: for embedded formulas break after the equals sign; for displayed formulas break before the equals sign. Consider changing math to improve layout where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sentence rhythm with punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semicolons and periods strategically to control reading speed and rhythm; break paragraphs to improve flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing semicolons to periods (or vice versa) and splitting paragraphs can improve pace, but preserve clarity and ensure any conjunction-starting sentences are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make variable names unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid misleading or overly similar variable names for conceptually unrelated entities; systematic renaming is helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use text editors to perform systematic renaming. Choose names that reflect roles and avoid confusion for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: State facts that remain true in the present tense; use past tense for claims later shown false or historically proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tense choice signals whether a fact is considered perpetually true or contextually/time-bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slashed fractions when stacked form shrinks digits
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overuse of stacked fractions with horizontal bars (which can produce tiny superscripts); consider slash form ((1+x)/y) and add parentheses when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors often convert stacked fractions to slashed form and add parentheses; be mindful of readability in exponents and nested fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clear, unambiguous exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises have little context and so must avoid ambiguity; include carefully chosen redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because exercises are hard to translate and have less context, provide extra clarifying information to ensure the intended interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit sources for exercises and historical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Give credit to previously published exercises and trace theorem histories where possible; copyright law encourages crediting sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing origins can be hard (historical omissions common), but crediting sources is generally sufficient and advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false displayed equations without warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not display false equations as if they were true; instead embed them in text with an explicit warning ('the equation ... is always false!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers may take displayed equations at face value; mark intentionally false or illustrative equations clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page breaks in the middle of displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure displayed formulas are not split across pages; add material to fill page or adjust layout so the entire display moves to the next page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near final edits, restructure text to prevent page breaks inside displays — treating it as a layout constraint that may require adding filler text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hyphen, en-dash, minus sign, em-dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Use different dash characters for distinct purposes: hyphen (shortest), en-dash (ranges, e.g., 10–18), minus sign (in formulae), em-dash (longest, in sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use them interchangeably; correct glyph usage improves typographic and mathematical clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent display style for integrals and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a convention for integral limit placement (limits above/below vs. at the right) and apply it consistently across a book, acknowledging tradeoffs between vertical and horizontal space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are used in practice; pick one that suits the format (narrow or wide text) and maintain consistency unless there's a compelling reason to vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present algorithms as readable literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat programs as literature: present algorithms in an English-labeled-step style (like theorems), include high-level flow charts, and use comments/invariants for correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting programs as raw code without exposition. Number steps, give parenthetical invariant remarks, and motivate modules at the psychologically right moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer language-neutral algorithm presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid tying algorithm exposition to a specific programming language to prevent alienating readers; explain algorithms in English or a high-level pseudo-style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a language may restrict audience or appear outdated; a language-neutral presentation is often more inclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: WEB/literate-programming module guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should be introduced at the psychologically right moment, be of manageable size (~a dozen lines of code), and include an informal but clear description of what it does (not a play-by-play).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break complex code into tractable parts; module descriptions should convey intuition and high-level behavior, not low-level stepping. Cut long modules into smaller ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Name modules with imperatives for action-like modules (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and descriptors for declarative-purpose modules (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting'); capitalize the first letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent and choose a naming style that reflects the module's function; prefer imperatives for operational modules and descriptors for sets of declarations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier readability in code
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid awkward capitalization patterns in identifiers (e.g., 'FindinNew Word3'); use underscores to conjoin words or other readable conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readable identifiers; WEB allows short underscores (which TANGLE may remove) to improve printed readability; very long identifiers (40+ chars) can also be clear if meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixed-width type for displayed code
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer fixed-width fonts for displayed computer programs to preserve alignment and readability; mixing roman, bold, and italic may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variable-width fonts can be unsuitable for program listings; insist on fixed-width where alignment matters, while balancing typographic needs for surrounding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent voice when describing program behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to anthropomorphize program actions ('it inserts') or use first-person plural ('we insert') and remain consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don favors 'we' as the narrator for program behavior; choose a voice and apply it consistently throughout documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting a new style (e.g., WEB), do not persistently carry over conventions from older styles that are no longer appropriate (e.g., redundant 'end { while }' comments unnecessary in WEB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reevaluate prior habits when moving to new systems; drop baggage that reduces clarity or conflicts with new conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide high-level module descriptions, not low-level play-by-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Module documentation should convey the intuition and purpose of a module rather than a detailed line-by-line walkthrough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a concise, informal description that helps the reader understand what the module does and why, enabling them to grasp the algorithm's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with symbols (e.g., 'data assumes that...'); rephrase sentences so they begin with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences starting with symbols are often awkward and can be rewritten to improve readability.
